newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia reports surge in massacres and 'terrorism'.
newsitem.headline: Colombia reports surge in massacres and 'terrorism'.

text.p: Colombia, often described as being among the bloodiest countries in the world, suffered a huge increase in violent crime led by massacres in the first three months of 1997, a senior police official said on Friday.

The number of massacres -- four or more victims in a single murder -- jumped a spine-chilling 128 percent over the first quarter of 1996, Brig. Gen. Ismael Trujillo, head of Colombia's Judicial Police, told a news conference.

Official police statistics he presented showed 72 people were killed in massacres in the first three months of 1996 compared to 164 in January-March 1997. Acts of "terrorism," which the police normally define as bombings by leftist guerrilla groups and drug gangs, rose 46 percent during the same time period, the statistics showed.

Trujillo did not apportion blame for the alarming increase in massacres, saying only that they were a result of the country's "internal conflict." Gunmen of the left and right have killed with impunity for years on the sidelines of Colombia's long-running guerrilla war but human rights groups have attributed most collective murders so far this year to a surge in activity by right-wing paramilitary groups.

Trujillo said the spiral of violence "surpasses society's capacity to counteract the problem," adding that Colombia's rate of violent crime was unequalled anywhere. "In Colombia the notion of the value of human life has largely been lost."

The statistics showed an average of four kidnappings every day during the first quarter of the year and a daily average of 68 murders and 16 fatalities in traffic accidents in a country of nearly 40 million people described in a recent World Bank report as the most violent place in Latin America.
